1.title: Responsible AI
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Responsible A I. It covers the exam area Identify A I concepts and capabilities. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Describe considerations for fairness in an A I solution. Describe considerations for reliability and safety in an A I solution. Describe considerations for privacy and security in an A I solution. Describe considerations for inclusiveness in an A I solution. Describe considerations for transparency in an A I solution. Describe considerations for accountability in an A I solution. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Identify A I concepts and capabilities (forty to forty-five percent). Exam format: a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes; check the exam page for the time. Validated against: the official A I nine oh one study guide, current skills measured.

1.title: The six principles
1.text: The six principles. Microsoft's approach to responsible A I is built on six principles. Each question on this topic gives a situation and asks which principle it touches. Fairness. Microsoft's one-line statement: A I systems should treat all people fairly. The question it answers: Does the system treat similar people in similar ways? Reliability and safety. Microsoft's one-line statement: A I systems should perform reliably and safely. The question it answers: Does it work as intended, and can it cause harm? Privacy and security. Microsoft's one-line statement: A I systems should be secure and respect privacy. The question it answers: Is personal data protected and used with permission?

1.title: The six principles, continued
1.text: The six principles. Inclusiveness. Microsoft's one-line statement: A I systems should empower everyone and engage all people, regardless of their backgrounds. The question it answers: Can everyone use it, including people with disabilities? Transparency. Microsoft's one-line statement: A I systems should be understandable. The question it answers: Do people know how it works, what it can and cannot do? Accountability. Microsoft's one-line statement: People should be accountable for A I systems. The question it answers: Who is responsible, and who can step in? Exam tip: Remember the first letters: Fairness, Reliability and safety, Privacy and security, Inclusiveness, Transparency, Accountability. Match the problem in the scenario to the principle.

1.title: The six principles, continued
1.text: The six principles. The figure shows this: The six responsible A I principles and the question each one asks.

1.title: Fairness
1.text: Fairness. Fairness means the system should not favor or disadvantage groups of people without a good reason. Typical risk: a model trained on biased or unbalanced data gives worse results for some groups, for example a loan or hiring model that learned a historical bias. Considerations: use representative training data, test results for different groups, and review the model for bias before and after release. Clue words: "different results for different groups", "bias", "treats applicants unequally". Exam tip: Match the problem in the scenario to the principle: unequal results for groups is fairness; wrong or harmful output is reliability and safety.

1.title: Reliability and safety
1.text: Reliability and safety. Reliability and safety means the system should work as designed, handle unexpected conditions and not cause harm. Typical risk: a system gives wrong answers, fails in conditions it was not tested for, or produces harmful content. Considerations: rigorous testing, handling of errors and unusual inputs, monitoring after release, and a way to turn the system off or fall back to a person. For generative A I, also filtering harmful output and checking for made-up answers (called hallucinations). Clue words: "must work in all conditions", "could harm someone if wrong", "testing", "safety".

1.title: Privacy and security
1.text: Privacy and security. Privacy and security means the system should protect data and respect people's privacy. Typical risk: training or using personal data without permission, leaking data in outputs, or letting attackers reach the system. Considerations: collect only what is needed, get consent, secure stored and transmitted data, control access, and follow data-protection rules. Clue words: "personal information", "consent", "data leaks", "protect customer data".

1.title: Inclusiveness
1.text: Inclusiveness. Inclusiveness means the system should empower and engage everyone, including people with disabilities, different languages or different backgrounds. Typical risk: a solution built only for a narrow group, such as a voice assistant that fails on some accents or an app that cannot be used with a screen reader. Considerations: design with people of different abilities and backgrounds, offer alternatives (captions, speech, text), and test with diverse users. Clue words: "accessible", "people with disabilities", "different languages and accents", "everyone can use it". Exam tip: Do not mix up transparency (the system is understandable) with accountability (people are responsible for it).

1.title: Transparency
1.text: Transparency. Transparency means people should understand how the system works and what its limits are. Typical risk: users do not know they are talking to an A I, or cannot tell why a decision was made. Considerations: tell users when A I is used, explain what the system can and cannot do, document how it was built and tested, and where possible give reasons for results. Clue words: "explain how the decision was made", "users should know it is A I", "documentation".

1.title: Accountability
1.text: Accountability. Accountability means people stay responsible for A I systems and their effects. Typical risk: nobody owns the outcome, or decisions are left entirely to the machine. Considerations: human oversight, clear roles and responsibility, governance and review processes, and a way to audit and correct the system. Clue words: "who is responsible", "human review", "governance", "oversight".

1.title: Responsible AI for generative AI
1.text: Responsible A I for generative A I. Generative A I adds risks that fit the same principles. Made-up facts (hallucinations). Principle it touches: Reliability and safety. Example response: Ground answers in trusted data; ask people to check. Harmful or offensive output. Principle it touches: Reliability and safety. Example response: Content filters and safety settings in the platform. Revealing private data. Principle it touches: Privacy and security. Example response: Do not put secrets or personal data in prompts; control access. Biased wording or images. Principle it touches: Fairness. Example response: Test with varied prompts and review outputs. Users unaware text is A I-written. Principle it touches: Transparency. Example response: Label A I-generated content. No human check on important output. Principle it touches: Accountability. Example response: Keep a person in the loop. Microsoft Foundry offers safety and guardrail settings that help with filtering harmful content. for current names and options.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors discovers that its résumé-screening model rejects applicants from one region more often. Which principle is mainly affected? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Fairness. Different results for different groups of applicants is a fairness concern.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A voice assistant fails to understand people with some accents or speech differences. Which principle is mainly affected? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Inclusiveness. Inclusiveness asks that the system works for everyone, regardless of background or ability.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A company tells users that an answer was written by A I and publishes what the system can and cannot do. Which principle does this support? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Transparency. Being open about the use and limits of A I supports transparency.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A team makes sure a named manager reviews high-impact A I decisions and can overrule them. Which principle does this support? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Accountability. People stay responsible and in control: that is accountability.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A chatbot sometimes states false facts with confidence, and testers add checks before release. Which principle is mainly affected? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Reliability and safety. A system that gives wrong or harmful output is a reliability and safety concern.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. An engineer pastes customer names and addresses into a public tool to test a prompt. Which principle is mainly at risk? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Privacy and security. Putting personal data where it should not go is a privacy and security risk.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Name the six responsible A I principles. Answer: Fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, accountability. Question two. Which principle says people should be accountable for A I systems? Answer: Accountability. Question three. Which principle covers people with disabilities being able to use a system? Answer: Inclusiveness.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is a hallucination? Answer: A confident answer from a generative model that is made up or wrong. Question five. Which principle says A I systems should be understandable? Answer: Transparency. Question six. Biased training data is mainly a problem for which principle? Answer: Fairness.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Fairness: treat people fairly; watch biased data; test for different groups. Reliability and safety: work as designed, handle surprises, no harm; testing, monitoring, filters. Privacy and security: protect data, consent, least data, access control. Inclusiveness: everyone can use it: disabilities, languages, accents. Transparency: understandable: say it is A I, explain limits and reasons. Accountability: people stay responsible: oversight, governance, audit. In the next module, we continue the course.
